blockMcqs.question: Which half of a core executes instructions out of order?
blockMcqs.explanation: The back-end schedules, executes out of order, and retires results; the front-end just fetches and decodes in order.

blockMcqs.question: What does register renaming remove?
options: False dependencies from reused register names
The need for a reorder buffer
blockMcqs.explanation: Mapping architectural names onto more physical registers kills false dependencies, letting independent uops run in parallel.

blockMcqs.question: What does a reservation station hold a uop until?
blockMcqs.explanation: A uop issues to an execution port as soon as its inputs are ready, not in program order.

blockMcqs.question: When does a uop retire from the reorder buffer?
options: As soon as it finishes executing
Once all older ROB entries have retired
When it enters the reservation station
blockMcqs.explanation: Retirement always happens in program order, even though execution itself finishes out of order.

blockMcqs.question: What does a TLB cache?
blockMcqs.explanation: The TLB avoids a full page-table walk by caching recent address translations.

blockMcqs.question: What does SMT (Hyper-Threading) actually share between threads?
options: Nothing — each gets a full separate core
The front-end, ports, and reservation stations
blockMcqs.explanation: SMT threads share most execution hardware but keep separate architectural register state, so gains are modest, not 2x.

blockMcqs.question: Why do wider cores see diminishing IPC returns?
options: Real code lacks enough independent instructions to fill more ports
The ISA forbids more execution ports
Branch prediction is no longer used
blockMcqs.explanation: Limited natural ILP in typical programs means extra ports and buffers often sit idle.

blockMcqs.question: What happens when reservation stations are full?
options: New uops stall and can't issue yet
blockMcqs.explanation: A full reservation station blocks new uops from entering, capping achievable overlap.

blockMcqs.question: What makes a memory access most expensive?
options: A TLB and cache hit at every level
A miss at both the TLB and all cache levels
Using an L1 cache at all
blockMcqs.explanation: Missing the TLB and every cache level forces a page-table walk plus a trip to main memory, costing hundreds of cycles.
